digest.top_line: SIB-CRT for LARC: 9-yr OS 74.3% vs 48.9% (HR 0.43, P=0.008) off a 56-60 Gy boost, with pCR flat and no toxicity cost.
digest.tldr: Lower-GI carries the day, and it is a dose question: a 106-pt randomized phase 2 missed its pCR primary endpoint yet separated on every 9-yr survival endpoint, LC 87.1% vs 70.1% (HR 0.40). MFS moving as hard as LC (HR 0.48) is the part that does not follow from a local boost.

sites.intro: Single trial, and it argues the pCR surrogate is the wrong readout for a rectal boost.

studies.name: SIB-CRT vs Standard CRT for LARC (NCT02195141)
studies.tldr: 9-yr OS 74.3% vs 48.9% (HR 0.43, P=0.008) with SIB dose escalation to 56-60 Gy, despite identical pCR.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase 2, N=106 (55 SIB-CRT / 51 CRT), stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma, accrued Aug 2013 to Feb 2015
🔍 RT: both arms 50 Gy/25 fx to pelvis; SIB arm added 56 Gy to PGTV and 60 Gy to lateral metastatic nodes when present
🔍 Radical surgery planned 6-8 wks post-CRT; median f/u 116.6 mo
📊 1° EP pCR was NEGATIVE: 15.2% vs 18.4%, P=0.695. Every survival endpoint is secondary
📊 Acute G3 toxicity 14.5% SIB-CRT vs 19.6% CRT, mostly radiation dermatitis. No toxicity cost to the boost
📊 Curative treatment (radical surgery or W&W) reached in 89.1% (49/55) vs 78.4% (40/51), P=0.135
⚠️ MFS moved as much as LC (HR 0.48 vs 0.40), which a local dose boost should not do. Distant control is the harder claim
⚠️ Subgroup: benefit confined to pts who got NO perioperative chemo (9-yr DFS 70.8%, HR 0.343, P=0.014); no added benefit with chemo. Exploratory, hypothesis-generating
⚠️ N=106 phase 2 with a negative 1° EP; 9-yr survival separations of 23-25 absolute points off ~50 pts/arm are fragile to a handful of events

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase 2, N=106, primary endpoint (pCR) not met; survival gains are secondary endpoints with wide event-count fragility. Confirmatory phase 3 needed before dose escalation changes practice.
verdict.audience: Stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma, neoadjuvant chemoradiation candidates

studies.significance: The boost was modest and deliverable on standard IMRT, 56 Gy to PGTV and 60 Gy to involved lateral nodes on a 50 Gy/25 fx pelvis, with acute G3 toxicity no higher (14.5% vs 19.6%). It moves the dose-escalation question in chemo-ineligible pts, where the DFS benefit concentrated (HR 0.343, P=0.014).
studies.monday_clinic: In stage II/III rectal cancer where perioperative chemotherapy is not an option, this supports discussing an integrated boost to the primary and involved lateral nodes; it does not extend to pts receiving full TNT-style systemic therapy, where no added benefit appeared.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **randomized phase 2**, 1:1, **N=106** (55 SIB-CRT, 51 CRT), accrued Aug 2013 to Feb 2015. Median follow-up **116.6 months**, unusually long for a rectal dose-escalation trial.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma** planned for neoadjuvant chemoradiation then radical surgery. Perioperative chemotherapy was not mandated, which becomes the axis of the key subgroup.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms **50 Gy/25 fx to the pelvis**. The experimental arm added a simultaneous integrated boost of **56 Gy to PGTV** and **60 Gy to lateral metastatic nodes** when present. Surgery **6-8 weeks** after chemoradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: pCR rate.** Secondary: DFS, OS, MFS, local control, cancer-specific survival, toxicity. The reported long-term separations therefore all sit on secondary endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Primary endpoint negative**: pCR 15.2% vs 18.4%, P=0.695. Every 9-year survival and control endpoint favored SIB-CRT (see table); curative treatment rate 89.1% vs 78.4% did not reach significance (P=0.135).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute grade 3 toxicity **14.5% (SIB-CRT) vs 19.6% (CRT)**, predominantly radiation dermatitis. **No toxicity penalty** for the boost in the acute window; late toxicity is not reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Dose escalation in LARC has repeatedly bought pCR without survival (the RECTAL-BOOST randomized trial found no improvement in its endpoint), and the field moved toward systemic intensification with RAPIDO and PRODIGE-23 rather than higher RT dose. This trial inverts that pattern: **no pCR gain but a large survival gain**, the opposite of the usual dose-escalation signature.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma treated with long-course chemoradiation and planned radical surgery, particularly pts not receiving perioperative chemotherapy. Does not represent TNT-treated pts, cT4/beyond-TME disease, or short-course regimens.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Single trial of ~50 pts per arm generating 23-25 point absolute survival gaps, a magnitude larger than modern phase 3 systemic intensification produced, so a small imbalance in events or baseline stage could carry it. The chemo-naive subgroup is exploratory and unpowered, and the 2013-2015 accrual predates routine TNT.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The internal logic is strained: a boost confined to PGTV and lateral nodes plausibly explains the **LC gain (87.1% vs 70.1%)**, but MFS moved nearly as much (HR 0.48), which requires either that local failure seeded distant disease or that the arms differed in something unmeasured. The result argues dose escalation deserves a properly powered phase 3, not that it is established.

studies.interpretation:
The strangest thing about this trial is what did not move. Dose escalation in locally advanced rectal cancer has a consistent signature in the literature: more dose buys more pathological response, and the survival curves then fail to follow. Here the signature is exactly inverted. pCR was flat (15.2% vs 18.4%, P=0.695), the endpoint the trial was actually powered for and the endpoint dose escalation is supposed to move, and yet at nearly ten years every survival and control measure separates by 20-plus absolute points. A reader should treat that inversion as the central question, not as a bonus finding, because the mechanism usually invoked for a boost, better tumor regression, is precisely the mechanism this trial failed to demonstrate.

There are two readings. The generous one is that pCR is a poor surrogate for what a boost achieves, that residual viable disease at the primary and in lateral nodes drives both local failure and later distant seeding, and that sterilizing it improves cure without changing the binary pathological readout. The local control result (87.1% vs 70.1%, HR 0.40) is the part of the data most consistent with that story and the part most mechanistically defensible for a radiation oncologist, since the boost volume and the failure site coincide. The skeptical reading is that an MFS hazard ratio of 0.48, nearly identical to the local control hazard ratio, is more than a 6 Gy boost to the primary should be able to deliver. Micrometastatic control by a pelvic boost is a strong claim, and the honest alternative is that a small randomized cohort produced correlated separations across every endpoint because of a modest imbalance in the underlying risk of the two arms.

Size is the constraint on confidence. Roughly fifty patients per arm followed to nine years generates survival differences larger than either RAPIDO or PRODIGE-23 achieved through full systemic intensification, which should give pause rather than reassurance. A treatment effect that outperforms the field's largest phase 3 efforts, delivered by a modest dose increment in a trial designed to answer a different question, is the profile of a result that regresses on replication. The curative treatment rate (89.1% vs 78.4%, P=0.135) hints that more SIB patients simply reached definitive local therapy, which would be a real benefit but a different one from radiobiological superiority.

The subgroup finding is where this becomes clinically usable and simultaneously most fragile. Benefit concentrated in patients who received no perioperative chemotherapy (9-year DFS 70.8%, HR 0.343, P=0.014) and vanished in those who did. That is biologically coherent, since escalated local therapy would matter most when systemic therapy is absent, but it is exploratory, unpowered, and drawn from an already small trial. What it usefully identifies is the population where the question remains genuinely open: patients who cannot tolerate or will not receive systemic intensification. In an era where the field's answer to rectal cancer has been TNT, the trial's own data suggest dose escalation adds nothing on top of chemotherapy, which narrows rather than broadens its reach.

For the boost to become practice it would need a phase 3 powered on disease-free survival rather than pCR, with late toxicity reported, in a chemo-ineligible or chemo-deferred population. Until then this is a signal worth carrying into a multidisciplinary discussion for the patient who will not get systemic therapy, not a reason to escalate dose generally.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The boost is modest and deliverable: 56 Gy to PGTV and 60 Gy to involved lateral nodes simultaneously integrated into a standard 50 Gy/25 fx pelvis, with acute G3 toxicity no higher (14.5% vs 19.6%). Local control 87.1% vs 70.1% (HR 0.40) is the mechanistically defensible part and moves the dose-escalation question in chemo-ineligible pts.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The benefit disappeared in pts who received perioperative chemotherapy and concentrated in those who did not (9-yr DFS 70.8%, HR 0.343, P=0.014). That argues escalated RT substitutes for, rather than adds to, systemic intensification, so it does not challenge a TNT strategy; it offers an option when chemotherapy is not deliverable.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Curative treatment (radical surgery or watch-and-wait) was reached in 89.1% vs 78.4% (P=0.135), with surgery planned at 6-8 weeks in both arms and pCR unchanged (15.2% vs 18.4%). The boost did not compromise resection timing or feasibility, and the local control gain bears on lateral nodal management.

papers.title: Dose-escalated versus Standard Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy for Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: 9-year Results of a Randomized Phase 2 Trial.
papers.journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the safety and efficacy of preoperative simultaneous integrated boost chemoradiotherapy (SIB-CRT) versus standard chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC).

METHODS AND MATERIALS: This prospective, randomized phase II trial (NCT02195141) enrolled patients with stage II/III rectal adenocarcinoma. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to CRT (50 Gy/25 fx to pelvis) or SIB-CRT (50 Gy/25 fx to the pelvis with SIB of 56 Gy to PGTV and 60 Gy to lateral metastatic nodes if present). Radical surgery was planned 6-8 weeks after chemoradiotherapy. The primary endpoint was pathological complete response (pCR) rate; secondary endpoints were disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), local control (LC), cancer-specific survival (CSS) and toxicity.

RESULTS: From August 2013 to February 2015, 106 patients were enrolled: 55 in the SIB-CRT group and 51 in the CRT group. Acute grade 3 toxicity occurred in 14.5% (SIB-CRT) and 19.6% (CRT) of patients, primarily manifested as radiation dermatitis. Curative treatment (radical surgery or watch-and-wait) was achieved in 89.1% (49/55) of SIB-CRT patients and 78.4% (40/51) of CRT patients (P=0.135). After a median follow-up of 116.6 months, the SIB-CRT group showed superior 9-year outcomes in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population: DFS (70.8% vs 47.4%; HR 0.46, P=0.013), OS (74.3% vs 48.9%; HR 0.43, P=0.008), MFS (70.8% vs 47.2%; HR 0.48, P=0.017), LC (87.1% vs 70.1%; HR 0.40, P=0.038) and CSS (77.4% vs 57.2%; P=0.027). Similar benefits were observed in the curative treatment cohort. The pCR rates were comparable (15.2% vs 18.4%; P=0.695). Exploratory subgroup analysis showed that the survival benefit of SIB-CRT was statistically significant in patients who did not receive perioperative chemotherapy (9-year DFS: 70.8%; HR=0.343, P = .014), whereas no additional benefit was observed in those receiving chemotherapy.

CONCLUSIONS: Dose escalation through SIB during neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy translates into superior long-term survival outcomes. Despite comparable pCR rates, the intensified control of both local disease and micrometastases by SIB-CRT, coupled with its significant superiority within the chemotherapy-naive subgroup, likely contributed to these robust results. These findings establish dose escalation as a potent strategy for optimizing long-term cure in the modern management of LARC, particularly in chemotherapy-ineligible patients.
